title: Closing Bell: CBA says AI snowball ready to roll downhill
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank reckons its investment in tech and artificial intelligence - and remember, it was a reasonably early AI adopter in corporate Australia - is about to start paying for itself.
The bank says "gross benefits" from AI use cases increased to $200 million in the year to June 30 and should double again to $400 million in the coming year, which means AI benefits should exceed AI investment for the first time.
In the bank's eyes, this marks an important inflection point. Tech spending/investing has increased to an Australian market-leading $2.4 billion a year, a 33 per cent increase since COVID-19, to a level where CBA thinks it can put a brick on it.
Which makes us wonder whether CBA has hit a peak on its tech investment and AI capex era when AI capex is still ballooning in the US.
"What we're saying is we can get more done," Comyn says. "We want to keep investment broadly flat year-on-year, and we expect to be able to get substantially more done for the benefit of our customers. AI is part of what's enabling that."
Comyn had a bunch of tech and AI benefits stats for investors at the group's results on Wednesday: 29 per cent improved banker productivity in business banking; 64 per cent more technology changes deployed; 45 per cent fewer major incidents; and 86 per cent success rate for chatbot conversations, all since FY24 when generative AI investment was just getting started.
Engineering velocity seems to be the big one - AI is allowing CBA to update its products and systems faster, cheaper and more frequently, snowballing on itself to the point where CBA thinks it is finally spending enough and can let its snowball run down the hill.
CBA's version of enough is a big number - $2.4 billion is about as much as WiseTech Global and Carsales owner Car Group collect in revenue each year combined, and is marginally ahead of Macquarie Group - to be the sector's biggest spender.
Two analysts asked questions about that $2.4 billion limit on Wednesday's earnings call, and you can bet the rest will also be talking to fund manager clients about it in the coming days as they try to work out whether it signals the start of Australian banking's big shift from tech spending/investing to harvesting and potentially a new productivity era.
The other thing investors are waiting for is revenue gains from AI - that's the holy grail.
CBA chief financial officer Alan Docherty, who seems to answer most analyst questions on earnings calls, said there were "revenue benefits emerging in both the retail bank and the business bank". "We're excited about a number of the pilot programs that we've got in place right now," he told analysts, pointing to Banker Workbench, which is used within the business bank to free up bankers to spend more time with clients.
Docherty says CBA's still in the investment phase, investing a little more than the benefits being realised, but that should turn in FY27. He says CBA could've cut spending but decided to keep it flat and, like his boss would also say, "get more done". (We should probably think about the $2.4 billion flat guidance in FY27 as a slight decline, in real terms).
Analysts like this inflection point story but are waiting to see overall improved productivity. The bank pointed to $404 million in "productivity" savings in FY26, roughly the same as one year prior, which suggests CBA isn't at its tech promised land just yet.
"In FY27, management guided that they will see an 'inflection point' where gross benefits exceed investment, but it remains to be seen whether this turns up in P&L benefits," Citi's Thomas Strong told clients after the earnings call. "Management indicated that of the [approximately] $400 million in current annual productivity, roughly 10 per cent was from AI investments - suggesting a way to go before meaningfully touching the sides."
The obvious question is what all this investment means for jobs and, unfortunately, we didn't get a chance to ask Comyn just that on Wednesday. The bank had 1 per cent more employees at the end of FY26 than it did a year earlier, according to Wednesday's disclosures. However, all this productivity talk and tech/AI investment is aimed at doing more with fewer resources in the future.
CBA shares dropped 1 per cent on Wednesday, but it was a solid result from a company that cannot afford any mishaps and particularly in its tech investment program, given the quantum of its spending, its management team's front-footedness in putting tech at the heart of its success story, the way analysts and fund managers can be cynical about capex programs and capitalising software costs, and the lack of growth in Australia's economy and perhaps banking's net interest income pie.
Shareholders should hope Comyn's right and, having invested heavily for years, all that tech investment is about to pay off.
Fairfax Media Management Pty Limited
